subject: Culture
title: Black Friday Frenzy
description: A fast breakdown of Black Friday Frenzy for builders.

hook.text: Black Friday has caused stampedes, fistfights, and at least 12 deaths since 2006. All for a discount.

buildup.text: The name originally described the chaos of post-Thanksgiving traffic in 1960s Philadelphia. Police coined it.

discovery.text: Retailers rebranded it as the day their books went 'into the black.' Profit turned a negative name positive.

twist.text: China's Singles' Day, November 11th, now outsells Black Friday. Alibaba made $84 billion in one day in 2021.

climax.text: Shopping holidays are engineered urgency. The deal isn't rare—the feeling of scarcity is the product.

punchline.text: The sale sells the panic, not the product.

quiz.question: Who originally coined the term 'Black Friday'?

details.summary: Black Friday — the day after American Thanksgiving — evolved from a local Philadelphia traffic problem into a global shopping frenzy. Retailers deliberately create scarcity and urgency, producing stampedes, fights, and billions in sales. It epitomizes how commerce manufactures cultural events.
details.whyItMatters: Black Friday reveals how consumer psychology and corporate strategy create cultural phenomena. Its global spread shows American commercial culture's extraordinary export power.
takeaways: The term Black Friday originally described post-Thanksgiving traffic chaos
Retailers generate billions in a single day through manufactured urgency
The tradition has spread to Europe, Asia, and Latin America

faq.question: Where does the term Black Friday come from?
faq.answer: Philadelphia police used 'Black Friday' in the 1960s to describe the chaotic day after Thanksgiving when suburban shoppers and football fans flooded the city. Retailers later rebranded it positively — claiming it was the day their accounts went from red (loss) to black (profit).

faq.question: Why has Black Friday spread globally?
faq.answer: American cultural influence, global e-commerce platforms (especially Amazon), and retailers' desire for a pre-Christmas sales boost drove worldwide adoption. Countries without Thanksgiving — including the UK, Germany, Brazil, and India — now hold Black Friday sales.
